warmup.q: A single thread loops over an ArrayList with for-each and calls list.remove(item) for one of the items. No other thread exists. What happens?
options: It silently skips the rest of the list
warmup.why: The exception has nothing to do with threads. The list's iterator keeps a count of structural changes, and the next call to next() sees that the list changed behind its back. One thread is enough. And the opposite surprise is worse: when two threads really do race on an ArrayList, the check is best effort, so you may get lost or corrupted data with no exception at all.

sections.h: ConcurrentHashMap is atomic per key, not per map
sections.html:
ConcurrentHashMap is the map to use when threads share one. Reads never lock. A write locks only the bin that its key hashes to, so writes to different keys mostly run in parallel. A write into an empty bin doesn't lock at all: it uses compare-and-set, as in the previous lesson.

Every single method is atomic. As lesson 3 of this track showed, a sequence of calls is not. So the map offers methods that do a whole read-modify-write on one key in one call:

  • putIfAbsent(k, v) inserts only if the key is missing.
  • computeIfAbsent(k, f) computes and inserts only if missing, and runs f at most once.
  • compute(k, f) and computeIfPresent(k, f) replace the value with f of the old one.
  • merge(k, v, f) inserts v, or replaces the old value with f(old, v).
  • replace(k, expected, next) is a compare-and-set on one key.

The Javadoc of each compute method says "The entire method invocation is performed atomically." That sentence is the reason to use them:

Java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> settledCents = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

void onSettled(String merchant, long cents) {
    settledCents.merge(merchant, cents, Long::sum);     // insert or add, atomically for this key
}

String issuerFor(String bin) {
    return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup);   // lookup runs at most once per BIN
}
Kotlin
val settledCents = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>()

fun onSettled(merchant: String, cents: Long) {
    settledCents.merge(merchant, cents, Long::plus)     // insert or add, atomically for this key
}

fun issuerFor(bin: String): String =
    issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup)       // lookup runs at most once per BIN

The figure shows why this scales. Two threads that update keys in different bins never meet. Two threads that update the same key take turns, which is exactly what you want.

Two more rules. ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values with NullPointerException. That is on purpose: when get(k) returns null, it always means "absent", so you never need a second call to tell "missing" from "mapped to null" (and a second call would be check-then-act). And Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) is no substitute. It has one lock for the whole map, and the same gap between calls.

try.title: Three maps, one count
steps: Read MapShootout. Eight threads record 800,000 payments across 1,000 merchants: on a HashMap with merge, on a ConcurrentHashMap with get-then-put, and on a ConcurrentHashMap with merge.

code.title: MapShootout.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** 8 threads count 800,000 payments over 1,000 merchants, three ways. Only one way is right. */ public class MapShootout { static void run(String label, Map<String, Integer> counts, Consumer<String> countOne) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; String[] error = new String[1]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); for (int n = 0; n < 100_000; n++) countOne.accept("m-" + (n % 1_000)); } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } }); ts[i].setDaemon(true); // a corrupted HashMap can even loop forever ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(5_000); long total = 0; try { for (int v : counts.values()) total += v; } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } System.out.printf("%-32s total %,9d of 800,000 keys %,5d of 1,000%s%n", label, total, counts.size(), error[0] == null ? "" : " threw " + error[0]); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<String, Integer> plain = new HashMap<>(); run("HashMap.merge", plain, k -> plain.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); Map<String, Integer> chm1 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap get then put", chm1, k -> chm1.put(k, chm1.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1)); Map<String, Integer> chm2 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap.merge", chm2, k -> chm2.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); } }

alt.title: MapShootout.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 threads count 800,000 payments over 1,000 merchants, three ways. Only one way is right. private fun run(label: String, counts: MutableMap<String, Int>, countOne: (String) -> Unit) { val go = CountDownLatch(1) var error: String? = null val ts = List(8) { thread(isDaemon = true) { // a corrupted HashMap can even loop forever try { go.await() repeat(100_000) { n -> countOne("m-${n % 1_000}") } } catch (e: Throwable) { error = e.javaClass.simpleName } } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join(5_000) } val total = try { counts.values.sumOf { it.toLong() } } catch (e: Throwable) { error = e.javaClass.simpleName; 0L } println("%-32s total %,9d of 800,000 keys %,5d of 1,000%s".format(label, total, counts.size, error?.let { " threw $it" } ?: "")) } fun main() { val plain = HashMap<String, Int>() run("HashMap.merge", plain) { k -> plain.merge(k, 1, Int::plus) } val chm1 = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Int>() run("ConcurrentHashMap get then put", chm1) { k -> chm1[k] = (chm1[k] ?: 0) + 1 } val chm2 = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Int>() run("ConcurrentHashMap.merge", chm2) { k -> chm2.merge(k, 1, Int::plus) } }

try.expect: The HashMap loses most of the counts, and usually one of its threads dies with ConcurrentModificationException (HashMap.merge notices the map changed while it worked). In runs here it kept 100,000 to 200,000 of 800,000. ConcurrentHashMap with get-then-put loses a few thousand: every call is safe, the pair isn't. Only ConcurrentHashMap.merge gives exactly 800,000.

sections.h: Keep the function short, and never touch the map from inside it
sections.html:
The function you pass to compute, merge or computeIfAbsent runs while the map holds the lock for that key's bin. Three things follow from that.

First, other writes to the same bin wait for your whole function. The Javadoc says so: "Some attempted update operations on this map by other threads may be blocked while computation is in progress, so the computation should be short and simple." An 80 ms call to the issuer directory inside computeIfAbsent makes every write that lands in that bin wait 80 ms. Reads are not blocked. For a cache that loads each key once, that is often fine. When it isn't, the worked example shows how to keep the slow work outside the map.

Second, the function must not change the map. The Javadoc is blunt again: "The mapping function must not modify this map during computation." Memoized recursion is how people break this rule without noticing:

Java
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2));   // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside
}
Kotlin
fun fib(n: Int): Long {
    if (n < 2) return n.toLong()
    return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) }   // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside
}

On JDK 21, ConcurrentHashMap throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update here, and HashMap throws ConcurrentModificationException. The JDK only catches some of these cases, so don't count on an exception. Compute the value outside the map, or build the table bottom-up.

Third, if the function throws, nothing is stored and the exception reaches the caller, so the next call tries again. If it returns null, nothing is stored either. The lab relies on that.

try.title: Break the rule on purpose
steps: Run RecursiveUpdate. It computes fib(30) with memoized recursion on a ConcurrentHashMap, then on a HashMap, then bottom-up.
Read the exception messages. Which map tells you what you did wrong?

code.title: RecursiveUpdate.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. */ public class RecursiveUpdate { static Map<Integer, Long> memo; static long fib(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // modifies the map from inside compute } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Map<Integer, Long> m : List.<Map<Integer, Long>>of(new ConcurrentHashMap<>(), new HashMap<>())) { memo = m; try { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": fib(30) = " + fib(30)); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": threw " + e); } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call Map<Integer, Long> table = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of(0, 0L, 1, 1L)); for (int n = 2; n <= 30; n++) table.put(n, table.get(n - 1) + table.get(n - 2)); System.out.println("bottom-up: fib(30) = " + table.get(30)); } }

alt.title: RecursiveUpdate.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. private lateinit var memo: MutableMap<Int, Long> private fun fib(n: Int): Long { if (n < 2) return n.toLong() return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) } // modifies the map from inside compute } fun main() { for (m in listOf<MutableMap<Int, Long>>(ConcurrentHashMap(), HashMap())) { memo = m try { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: fib(30) = ${fib(30)}") } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: threw $e") } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call val table = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf(0 to 0L, 1 to 1L)) for (n in 2..30) table[n] = table.getValue(n - 1) + table.getValue(n - 2) println("bottom-up: fib(30) = ${table[30]}") }

try.expect: ConcurrentHashMap: threw java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update, HashMap: threw java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, and bottom-up: fib(30) = 832040. Only the version that fills the table outside any compute call works.

sections.h: Weak iterators, estimated sizes, and what ConcurrentModificationException means
sections.html:
ConcurrentModificationException sounds like "two threads touched my collection". It means something narrower: this collection's own iterator noticed that the collection changed in a way the iterator didn't make. ArrayList and HashMap iterators are fail-fast. They keep a count of changes and check it on every next(). One thread is enough to trip it, as the warm-up showed. And the check is best effort: when two threads race, it may not fire at all, and you get lost entries or a damaged structure instead. Never treat the exception as a race detector.

The concurrent collections have weakly consistent iterators. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, and they reflect the collection at some point at or after the moment the iterator was created. A change made during the loop may or may not show up.

The same goes for size(), isEmpty() and containsValue() on ConcurrentHashMap. While other threads update the map, they describe a moving target. The Javadoc calls them useful for monitoring and estimation, not for program control. if (map.size() < 10_000) map.put(k, v) is check-then-act on an estimate.

CopyOnWriteArrayList takes the opposite trade. Every write copies the whole array. Every iterator walks the array as it was when the loop started, so iteration never locks and never throws. That is perfect for a list of webhook listeners that changes at deploy time and is iterated on every payment. It is terrible for a list that grows with traffic: adding the 100,000th element copies 100,000 references. CopyOnWriteArraySet works the same way, and ConcurrentSkipListMap is the concurrent sorted map.

try.title: Trip a fail-fast iterator with one thread
steps: Read FailFast. It modifies an ArrayList, a ConcurrentHashMap and a CopyOnWriteArrayList while iterating over each one, all on the main thread.
Predict what each line prints. In the copy-on-write loop, the body adds an item for every item it sees: does the loop ever end?

code.title: FailFast.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. */ public class FailFast { public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside for-each List<String> pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); try { for (String p : pending) { if (p.equals("pay-2")) pending.remove(p); // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("ArrayList, one thread: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws Map<String, Integer> open = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("pay-1", 1, "pay-2", 2, "pay-3", 3, "pay-4", 4)); for (String k : open.keySet()) { if (k.equals("pay-2")) open.remove(k); if (k.equals("pay-3")) open.put("pay-5", 5); // may or may not show up in this loop } System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now " + open.size() + " keys"); // 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList: the loop walks a snapshot taken when it started List<String> hooks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c")); int seen = 0; for (String h : hooks) { hooks.add(h + "+"); // goes into a NEW array seen++; } System.out.println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: loop saw " + seen + " items, list now has " + hooks.size()); // 4. the single-thread fix for case 1: remove through the iterator, or removeIf pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); pending.removeIf(p -> p.equals("pay-2")); System.out.println("ArrayList.removeIf: " + pending); } }

alt.title: FailFast.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. fun main() { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside a for loop var pending = mutableListOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4") try { for (p in pending) { if (p == "pay-2") pending.remove(p) // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("ArrayList, one thread: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws val open = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf("pay-1" to 1, "pay-2" to 2, "pay-3" to 3, "pay-4" to 4)) for (k in open.keys) { if (k == "pay-2") open.remove(k) if (k == "pay-3") open["pay-5"] = 5 // may or may not show up in this loop } println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now ${open.size} keys") // 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList: the loop walks a snapshot taken when it started val hooks = CopyOnWriteArrayList(listOf("a", "b", "c")) var seen = 0 for (h in hooks) { hooks.add("$h+") // goes into a NEW array seen++ } println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: loop saw $seen items, list now has ${hooks.size}") // 4. the single-thread fix for case 1: remove through the iterator, or removeIf pending = mutableListOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4") pending.removeIf { it == "pay-2" } println("ArrayList.removeIf: $pending") }

try.expect: The ArrayList throws ConcurrentModificationException with one thread. The ConcurrentHashMap loop throws nothing and ends with 4 keys. The copy-on-write loop sees 3 items and ends, while the list now has 6, because the loop walks the snapshot it started with. removeIf is the single-thread fix for the first case.

sections.h: BlockingQueue is the collection for handing work between threads
sections.html:
Lesson 5 of this track built a bounded buffer by hand. ArrayBlockingQueue is the production version, and every BlockingQueue offers the same four ways to add and remove:

Throws Returns a special value Blocks Times out
Insert add(e) offer(e): false if full put(e) offer(e, time, unit)
Remove remove() poll(): null if empty take() poll(time, unit)
Examine element() peek(): null if empty

Pick the column by what the caller should do when the queue is full or empty. A request thread usually wants offer and an answer now. A dedicated consumer thread wants take and sleeps until there is work. Queues reject null because poll uses null to mean "empty".

The implementations differ in ways that matter in production:

  • ArrayBlockingQueue is bounded, backed by one array and one lock.
  • LinkedBlockingQueue takes an optional capacity, and the default is Integer.MAX_VALUE. That is unbounded in practice. It uses separate locks for the head and the tail, so producers and consumers contend less.
  • SynchronousQueue has no capacity at all. Each put waits for a take, and offer with no waiting taker returns false.
  • PriorityBlockingQueue orders by priority and is unbounded. DelayQueue releases each element only when its delay has passed.

A bounded queue gives you back-pressure. When the consumer falls behind, put makes the producer wait, or offer tells it to back off, so the system slows down instead of filling memory. drainTo(list, max) moves everything already queued in one call without waiting, which is how you batch. The lab's Batcher uses exactly that pair: poll with a timeout for the first entry, then drainTo for the rest.

try.title: Fill a queue every way you can
steps: Read QueueMethods. It fills an ArrayBlockingQueue of 2, then tries add, offer, timed offer and put on the full queue.
Predict each line, including the capacity of a LinkedBlockingQueue built with no arguments.

code.title: QueueMethods.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The four ways to add to a full BlockingQueue, and two queues that surprise people. */ public class QueueMethods { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<String> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2); q.put("e-1"); q.put("e-2"); // now full try { q.add("e-3"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("add: throws " + e); } System.out.println("offer: " + q.offer("e-3")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); boolean timed = q.offer("e-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.printf("offer(300 ms): %s after %d ms%n", timed, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); Thread producer = new Thread(() -> { try { q.put("e-3"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); producer.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("put: producer is " + producer.getState() + " until space opens"); System.out.println("take: " + q.take() + " (frees a slot)"); producer.join(); System.out.println("queue now: " + q); try { q.offer(null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("offer(null): throws NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() capacity: " + new LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()); System.out.println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: " + new SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("e-9")); } }

alt.title: QueueMethods.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The four ways to add to a full BlockingQueue, and two queues that surprise people. fun main() { val q: BlockingQueue<String> = ArrayBlockingQueue(2) q.put("e-1") q.put("e-2") // now full try { q.add("e-3") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("add: throws $e") } println("offer: ${q.offer("e-3")}") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val timed = q.offer("e-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println("offer(300 ms): $timed after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") val producer = thread { q.put("e-3") } Thread.sleep(200) println("put: producer is ${producer.state} until space opens") println("take: ${q.take()} (frees a slot)") producer.join() println("queue now: $q") // Kotlin won't even compile q.offer(null) on a BlockingQueue<String>; the JDK would throw NullPointerException println("LinkedBlockingQueue() capacity: ${LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()}") println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: ${SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("e-9")}") }

try.expect: add throws IllegalStateException: Queue full, offer returns false at once, the timed offer returns false after about 300 ms, and the producer in put is WAITING until take frees a slot. The no-argument LinkedBlockingQueue reports a capacity of 2,147,483,647. SynchronousQueue.offer returns false because nobody is waiting to take.

analogy: A ConcurrentHashMap is a bank with many tellers, one per group of account numbers. Customers with accounts in different groups are served at the same time; two customers for the same group queue at that one teller. Anyone may look at the balance board without queueing at all. A CopyOnWriteArrayList is a printed notice board: to change it, you print a whole new sheet and pin it up, and people reading the old sheet keep reading the old sheet. A bounded BlockingQueue is a coat check with 50 hooks: when they're full, the next guest waits or is told to come back later. The analogy breaks at the teller: a human teller would notice if you asked them to serve you while they were already serving you. computeIfAbsent calling itself only sometimes gets caught.
world: Most of these show up in a payment service within a week. A BIN or tenant-config cache is a ConcurrentHashMap with computeIfAbsent. Per-merchant totals for a settlement report are merge(merchant, cents, Long::sum), or computeIfAbsent(merchant, m -> new LongAdder()).increment() when the keys are hot. Webhook or fraud-rule listeners that change only at deploy time live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList. And the outbox relay that moves ledger entries from request threads to a single Kafka-producing thread is a BlockingQueue. Give it a capacity, and decide what a full queue means: block the producer, answer 503, or pause() the Kafka consumer that feeds it.
mistake: The most common real mistake is the unbounded queue. new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() looks harmless, and put never blocks, so it works in every test. Then the database slows down during an incident, the consumer falls behind, the queue grows to millions of entries, the garbage collector thrashes, and the pod is killed for running out of memory, taking every queued entry with it. Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses the same unbounded queue internally, which the executors track comes back to. The fix is to always pass a capacity and to decide, on purpose, what happens when the queue is full: put to slow the producer down, or offer to reject the work with a retryable error.

compare.title: Load-once caching in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> issuers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String issuerFor(String bin) { return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup); // lookup runs at most once per BIN }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: val issuers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>() fun issuerFor(bin: String): String = issuers.getOrPut(bin) { directory.lookup(bin) } // atomic put, but lookup may run several times fun issuerForOnce(bin: String): String = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin) { directory.lookup(it) } // lookup runs at most once per BIN

compare.note: Kotlin's idiomatic getOrPut is the trap. The standard library has a special version for ConcurrentMap that uses putIfAbsent, so it never overwrites a value that is already there. But its documentation says the default function "may be invoked even if the key is already in the map". With 8 threads racing for one new key, the lookup ran 8 times in a check here, against once for computeIfAbsent. And if the variable's declared type is plain MutableMap, Kotlin picks the general getOrPut, which is a check followed by a put with no atomicity at all. Use computeIfAbsent when the loader is slow or must run once. Kotlin's type system does help in one place: ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> can't be handed a null value, so the NullPointerException that Java callers can hit becomes a compile error.

worked.title: Load once, without holding the bin for 80 ms

steps.say: The issuer directory takes 80 ms. This cache loads each BIN once, which is good. But while it loads, every other write that lands in the same bin waits, and the Javadoc asks for short functions. The goal: keep the map operation tiny and do the slow work outside it, while still loading each BIN once.
steps.code: String issuerFor(String bin) { return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup); // 80 ms with the bin locked }

alt.html: fun issuerFor(bin: String): String = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup) // 80 ms with the bin locked

steps.say: Cache the promise of a value instead of the value. The function inside computeIfAbsent now only creates a CompletableFuture that starts the lookup on another pool. That takes microseconds, so the bin is free again almost at once. Every caller for the BIN gets the same future and waits on it outside the map.
steps.code: private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> issuers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String issuerFor(String bin) { // 1. claim the BIN: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds CompletableFuture<String> f = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, b -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> directory.lookup(b), ioPool)); try { return f.join(); // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (CompletionException e) { issuers.remove(bin, f); // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e; } }

alt.html: private val issuers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>>() fun issuerFor(bin: String): String { // 1. claim the BIN: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds val f = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin) { b -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ directory.lookup(b) }, ioPool) } try { return f.join() // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (e: CompletionException) { issuers.remove(bin, f) // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself: why remove(bin, f) with two arguments, and not remove(bin)? Answer: between the failure and the remove, another thread may already have put a fresh future in place of the failed one. The two-argument remove deletes the entry only if it still maps to the future that failed. It is a compare-and-set on one key, and it keeps you from throwing away someone else's good load.

This is the Memoizer from Java Concurrency in Practice, section 5.6, written with CompletableFuture. One gap is left: entries never expire, so a BIN that moves to a new issuer stays wrong until restart. A production service would use a caching library with expiry and asynchronous loading. Writing it once by hand tells you what that library does for you, and what to look for when it misbehaves.

lab.title: Three concurrent-collection fixes
steps: Run the tests. Six of eight fail: BinCache calls its loader 8 times for one BIN, WebhookRegistry throws ConcurrentModificationException (once even with a single thread), and Batcher throws UnsupportedOperationException.
Fix WebhookRegistry by changing the type of collection it uses. You don't need a lock.
Write Batcher on an ArrayBlockingQueue. submit uses offer. nextBatch waits with poll(timeout) for the first entry, then calls drainTo(batch, max - 1).
Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: computeIfAbsent takes the loader as it is: issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, loader). If the loader throws, nothing is stored, which is what the third test checks.

Why not Collections.synchronizedList for the registry? Its add and remove are safe, but you must hold its lock for the whole loop while iterating, and a listener that unregisters itself during publish still throws, on the same thread.
poll(timeout) returns null when time runs out. drainTo never waits; it moves only what is already there.
lab.done: All eight tests in ConcurrentCollectionsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A per-key counter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write DeclineCounter with record(String reason) and long count(String reason), safe for many threads, using a ConcurrentHashMap and one LongAdder per reason. Check: can two threads ever create two adders for the same reason?

answer.html: class DeclineCounter { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> byReason = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); void record(String reason) { byReason.computeIfAbsent(reason, r -> new LongAdder()).increment(); } long count(String reason) { LongAdder a = byReason.get(reason); return a == null ? 0 : a.sum(); } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class DeclineCounter { private val byReason = ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder>() fun record(reason: String) { byReason.computeIfAbsent(reason) { LongAdder() }.increment() } fun count(reason: String): Long = byReason[reason]?.sum() ?: 0L }

recap: ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin and never for reads. Single calls are atomic; sequences of calls are not.
Use computeIfAbsent, compute, merge, putIfAbsent and two-argument remove/replace for per-key read-modify-write.
The compute function runs under the bin's lock: keep it short, and never modify the map from inside it.
ConcurrentModificationException is a fail-fast iterator check, often tripped by one thread. Concurrent collections never throw it; their iterators and size() are weakly consistent.
CopyOnWriteArrayList suits small, rarely changed, often iterated lists, such as listeners.
Use a bounded BlockingQueue for hand-offs between threads. The no-argument LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "We switched to ConcurrentHashMap, so our cache and counters are thread-safe now." Explain what that does and doesn't buy them, with one example of each.
explain.answer: It buys them a map whose individual calls are safe from many threads: no corrupted structure, no lost entries from concurrent puts, reads that never block, and iteration that never throws. It does not make sequences of calls atomic. if (map.get(k) == null) map.put(k, load(k)) can still load twice, and map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1) can still lose counts. Those need the per-key atomic methods: computeIfAbsent and merge. They should also keep those functions short, never touch the map inside them, and not use size() for decisions while other threads write.

deeper.html:
Since JDK 8, ConcurrentHashMap is an array of bins. An empty bin is filled with a compare-and-set, with no lock. An update to a non-empty bin takes the monitor of the bin's first node with synchronized. That is why a long compute function blocks other writers in the same bin but nobody else. computeIfAbsent on an empty bin first installs a placeholder, a reservation node, and holds its lock while your function runs. A nested call that runs into a reservation node in the same thread is how the map detects many recursive updates and throws Recursive update.

A bin that collects 8 or more entries turns into a small red-black tree, as long as the table has at least 64 bins, so a bad hashCode degrades lookups to logarithmic time instead of linear. When the table grows, threads that try to write during the resize help move bins to the new table instead of waiting for it.

The size is kept the way LongAdder keeps a count: a base value plus counter cells that threads update under contention. That is why size() can't be an exact snapshot while writers are busy, and why mappingCount(), which returns a long, is the method the Javadoc prefers.

The map also has bulk operations that most people never find: forEach, search and reduce, each with a parallelismThreshold. settledCents.reduceValuesToLong(Long.MAX_VALUE, Long::longValue, 0L, Long::sum) sums all values on the calling thread; a small threshold such as 1 lets it split the work over the common fork-join pool. Like the iterators, these see a weakly consistent view, so a total taken while payments settle is close but not exact.
